activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: A journal's impact factor, devised by Eugene Garfield, is the average number of citations received in one year by articles the journal published in the previous two years.
story:
Cole set the two articles side by side on the kitchen table, one from a journal with a name so long it wrapped twice around the cover page, the other from something called Notes and Queries in Education. His laptop was open to a blank document with the cursor blinking at the top like something impatient. The assignment from Mr. Dela Cruz was due in two days, and all it said was: compare the two articles on class size and achievement, and take a position on which argument holds up better.

Soren dropped into the chair across from him without asking, which was how Soren did most things. He pulled the first article toward himself and read for about forty seconds.

"That's the one you lead with," he said. "It's from a big journal. The other one's from nowhere."

"It's from somewhere. It's just smaller."

"Big journals publish the good stuff. That's how it works. My brother says you check the impact factor and that settles it."

Cole had seen the number. The big journal's was something like eleven, printed proudly at the bottom of its homepage, next to a graph that trended upward. He had almost written his opening paragraph around it, a quick flourish of authority to forestall any doubt about his sources, before he'd actually looked up what the number counted. A journal's impact factor, devised by Eugene Garfield, was the average number of citations received in one year by articles the journal published in the previous two years. He read the definition twice on his phone, then a third time, because the first two readings hadn't done what the third one finally did.

"It's the average," he said.

"Average what?"

"Citations. For the whole journal, across everything it put out in the last two years. It's a number about the journal, not about the article." He turned the screen so Soren could see the sentence. "One paper could have been cited four hundred times and another in the same issue never at all, and they'd both live under the same average."

Soren read it, then pushed the phone back across the table, unbothered in the way of someone who intended to stay unbothered. "So the big journal still wins on average. Eleven beats whatever the small one has."

"That's not what average means for one article." Cole heard how much he sounded like a textbook and stopped. It wasn't Soren he was arguing with anyway. It was the paragraph he'd already drafted in his head, the one that opened by ranking his sources before it had said a single thing about them.

Kalli arrived with a bag of chips and her own homework, claimed the third chair, and asked what they were fighting about. When Cole explained, she said, "So the number's a shortcut."

"It's a shortcut that goes somewhere else."

She crunched a chip and considered both articles as if they were contestants. "So which one is actually better?"

That was the question, and it was worse than the number. Cole pulled both articles back in front of him and read the methods sections again, this time with a pen. The big-journal paper used a dataset of eleven districts and made a clean claim: class size didn't matter once teacher quality was controlled. The small-journal paper followed two districts for six years, couldn't control for much of anything, and refused to conclude more than that the effect seemed to depend on which students you were talking about. The first was sharper. The second was more careful. He had been planning to call the second one weaker, possibly as a kind of subterfuge, a way of seeming tough-minded by knocking down the impecunious journal with the smaller reputation. He could see now that the two moves were the same move: trusting the label over the argument.

He started typing anyway, because the deadline didn't care about his clarity. He wrote that the first article's design was stronger, and that its author had gone further than the design could carry. He wrote that the second article's limitations were honest ones, stated in the open, which was not the same as being wrong. He got to the end of a paragraph and then stopped, hands over the keys.

"I can't actually tell if I'm supposed to pick one," he said.

"You are," said Soren. "There's a rubric."

"The rubric says a considered position." Cole looked at the half page on his screen. "I can consider and still not land."

Kalli leaned over and read a few lines, chip dust on her fingers. "Then say that. Say the first one's probably more right and the second one's more honest about what it knows."

He typed for a while after that. When he finally looked up, the kitchen had gone dark except for the light over the table, and Soren was asleep with his cheek on the big journal's cover.

"Soren," Cole said. "You're drooling on the high impact factor."

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
knowledge_domain: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
fact: In a time signature, the top number gives the number of beats in each bar and the bottom number gives the note value that gets one beat, so 4/4 means four quarter-note beats.
story:
Delaney's kitchen table was littered with manuscript paper, a pencil sharpener shaped like a violin, and two mugs of tea gone cold. Anthony had been cajoled into this by a single text, sent at eleven the night before: my cousin's wedding needs a piece, tiny, sixteen bars, they'll pay me, you know theory better than I do. He had said no, then said fine, and now here he was on a Sunday afternoon with his knuckles aching from writing noteheads small enough to fit four of them in a bar.

The melody had come surprisingly fast. He'd hummed it in the car on the way over, something in D minor that reminded him of rain on a windshield, and Delaney had whooped and said it sounded like actual money. The trouble started when he tried to put it on the page. He wrote the first phrase, then the second, then stopped counting and just followed his ear, and when he finally sat back the tune looked right and felt right and was, according to the staff paper, a complete mess.

Delaney leaned over his shoulder, tapping each bar with the pencil. "Wait, why does this bar have five notes and the next one have three?" She counted again, mouthing the numbers. "What time signature is this even in?"

Anthony looked at the page as if it had betrayed him. He knew the answer in the abstract, the way he knew the capital of a country he'd never visited. "If it's 4/4, then every bar needs the same amount of beats," he said slowly. "Four of them." He drew the fraction at the start of the first line, then hesitated. "The top number tells you how many beats are in each bar. The bottom number tells you which note gets one beat. So the four on the bottom means a quarter note gets the beat." He said it out loud partly for her, mostly for himself, and heard immediately what it meant for his melody: the bars where he'd crammed five quarter notes were simply wrong, or at least wrong for 4/4, which was the only time signature he could reliably handle.

"Can't you just make some of them eighth notes?" Delaney asked. She was canny that way, allergic to redoing work, always hunting for the fix that cost the least. "Like, two of those five could share a beat."

He tried it. He tied two pairs together with beams and suddenly the bar added up, four beats with the last two divided, and the rhythm he'd been hearing in the car was actually there on the page for the first time. He felt a small, ridiculous thrill, the kind he usually hid. "That works," he said. "That actually works."

But two bars later the trick failed him. The phrase wanted to hold a note across where the barline sat, and when he moved the line to accommodate it, the whole opening shifted and the first phrase no longer ended where it used to. He pressed the pencil against the page without writing anything. For a while the only sound was Delaney's dog snoring under the table.

"You're doing the face," she said. "The face you did before the calc final."

"The music and the math are fighting," Anthony said. "What I hear doesn't fit evenly, and the notation only takes even. Or it takes uneven, but I don't know how to make it do that yet." He thought about Mr. Eze, who had told them once that a composer's education was mostly learning what your instincts were actually doing, and he'd thought it was a nice line and nothing more. Now it felt more like a subpoena, something he was being compelled to answer for. His ear had invented a rhythm with five in it somewhere, and the page had caught him.

He started a fresh sheet. On the second line, where the melody wanted its extra beat, he let the bar run long on purpose and wrote the whole phrase out with no barlines at all, like a confession. Then he counted, and counted again, and found that the phrase was eleven beats, which was close to twelve, which was three bars of four if he added one beat of rest. A rest. He'd been fighting to give every sound a symbol and never considered giving a silence one.

"One beat of nothing," he said, drawing the squiggle of a quarter rest into the gap, "and it all fits."

Delaney peered at it, counted the bars on her fingers, and frowned. "That's only fifteen bars. You need sixteen."

Anthony laughed, took the pencil back, and wrote a final whole note, four beats of a held D, filling the last bar completely.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: Early Action in US college admissions gives an early decision but is non-binding, so an admitted student may still choose not to enroll.
story:
The envelope had been sitting on Olivier's desk for two days, thick and cream-colored, and he had brought it to the guidance office unopened because he could not decide whether opening it alone was brave or stupid. Mr. Lindqvist's office smelled of burnt coffee and the lemon cleaner the janitor used on the floors after fourth period. Outside the frosted window, someone was dragging a lunch table across the courtyard, a long metallic scrape.

"You can open it here," Mr. Lindqvist said, not looking up from his keyboard. "Or you can sit there holding it until May. Both are options."

Olivier set the envelope on the desk between them, square and deliberate, like a move in a game he had not agreed to play. He had applied Early Action to Alder College in October, and the reply had arrived in December, and the other six applications, the ones his mother kept asking about, were due January first. He had not finished a single one.

Rocco had texted him that morning: "just open it dude. if its yes ur done. why would you keep writing essays." Then, a minute later: "unless its binding? is it binding? marc said its binding." Olivier had typed "not binding" and then deleted it, because he was not sure he knew what that meant, exactly, and he did not want Rocco building plans on something Olivier had half-heard in a hallway.

He opened it now, one thumb under the flap, and the paper inside was still crisp. "Congratulations," it began, and Mr. Lindqvist finally turned around in his chair.

"So you're in."

"I'm in." Olivier read the paragraph again, slower. Then he read the small print on the second page, the part everyone told you nobody read. It said the admission was an offer, not an obligation. It said an admitted student under Early Action was free to enroll or not enroll, the choice entirely his, and it said this in the flat language of institutions that did not care which way you fell.

He put the letter down. "I thought it was like a promise. You apply early, they answer early, and if it's yes, that's it, you're committed."

"Then you thought wrong," Mr. Lindqvist said, "which happens to everyone, and better now than later." He pulled a folder from the stack against the wall, Olivier's name on the tab. "You have nine days on the other applications. Financial aid packages come in spring. You compare."

Olivier sat with that. He had been imagining December as a door closing behind him, one way in, no way out, and the feeling had been almost a relief, a decision made by the calendar. Now the letter had handed the decision back, whole and unmade, and he understood that he would have to make it himself in April with numbers in front of him, and that this was both worse and better.

Layne found him at lunch, tray clattering down across from his. "Rocco says you got in and you're done, no more essays, we're going out Friday."

"It's not done," Olivier said. "Early Action gives you the answer early, but it doesn't hold you. I can still go somewhere else if the money's better somewhere else." He heard himself say it and recognized it was the first sentence of the whole business he had actually thought through.

"You're still writing essays," Layne said. It was not quite a question.

"I'm still writing essays."

Layne stole one of his fries, sanguine about it, as if the whole future were a matter of small thefts distributed evenly among friends. "My cousin got in early somewhere and just stopped. Didn't finish anything else. It worked out, I guess." A shrug that contained, Olivier thought, an entire litotes, a whole argument made of what Layne would not say about how it had not worked out.

That night he spread the six unfinished applications across his bed like a hand of cards he was being asked to play blind. The deadline was nine days away. His mother passed the doorway twice, said nothing, and did not abscond with his laptop, which he knew was her way of trusting him. He pulled the nearest laptop toward him, opened the document with the half-finished essay about his grandfather's workshop, and began typing where he had stopped, mid-sentence, in October.

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: Edmund Burke's Reflections on the Revolution in France, published in 1790, condemned the Revolution for destroying tradition, and set the conservative view that historians after 1800 argued with.
story:
Sophie had the museum's pamphlet folded into quarters and a photocopy of her essay prompt pressed flat on the table beside it. The prompt said: trace how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800. She had three paragraphs and no beginning.

Slade sat across from her in the café under the marble staircase, stirring a coffee he had no intention of drinking. "Just start with Burke," he said. "Everyone starts with Burke."

"That's the problem." She turned her notebook toward him. On the page she had written Burke, 1790, and drawn a box around it, then drawn a question mark outside the box. "The essay is about historians after 1800. His book came out in 1790. If I start there, I'm starting before my own period."

"So don't count him as a historian. Count him as the thing they're arguing with." Slade tapped the question mark. "He condemned the Revolution for destroying tradition. That's the conservative view. Everyone after him is either agreeing or fighting it."

Sophie looked at the pamphlet, which reproduced a page from a later edition of the Reflections in a glass case upstairs. She had stood in front of it for ten minutes before coming down. The book had been published in 1790, a year after the fall of the Bastille and a decade before her period opened, and it had set the position that later writers pushed against. That was what she had written in her notes: set the conservative view that historians after 1800 argued with. The phrasing was not hers. She had lifted it from a panel on the third floor and now could not tell whether she understood it or had merely copied it.

Leane arrived with a bag of postcards and dropped into the third chair. "Ms. Desir says your thesis has to make a claim, not a tour." She fanned the postcards across the table. "She told me that about mine. Twice."

"My thesis is a tour," Sophie said. "Paragraph one is the liberals, paragraph two is the Marxists, paragraph three is the revisionists. It's a list with dates."

"Then interpolate something," Leane said. "Put your own argument in between theirs."

Sophie wrote the word on the margin of her notebook, then crossed it out, then wrote it again. The problem was not the order of the paragraphs. The problem was that she did not yet have a position of her own to put between anyone else's. She believed the Revolution had been necessary and she believed it had been a catastrophe, and she had been treating those as two paragraphs rather than as one contradiction she might be allowed to hold.

They went back upstairs. The Burke exhibit was in a long room with the case at the far end, and Slade walked ahead while Leane stopped at a map of the provinces. Sophie read the panel again, alone. It quoted a line about the wreck of a state and mentioned the year of publication, 1790, without comment. She stood there working it through. Burke stood before 1800; the historians she was assigned stood after it; the assignment itself, "since 1800," drew a line that made Burke an ancestor rather than a member of the family. But an essay that opened with the descendant and only later produced the ancestor would lose the reader, and an essay that opened with the ancestor and apologized for the date would lose the argument. There was a third option, which was to open with the argument itself, the disagreement, and let Burke arrive as the first voice in it, arriving early the way he had in fact arrived early, before the century his critics lived in had even begun.

She sat down on the bench opposite the case and drafted a first sentence in her notebook. It began: To argue about the French Revolution after 1800 was, knowingly or not, to argue with Edmund Burke. She read it twice. It was parsimonious, one clause doing the work of her three flabby paragraphs, and she distrusted it for that reason, the way she distrusted anything that came out finished. Some sentences were thought; that one felt like a performance, a virtuoso opening she could not sustain for six more pages.

Slade came back and read over her shoulder. "So you're starting before 1800 anyway."

"I'm starting with the argument, not the date." She closed the notebook before she could revise the sentence again. "I'm not sure it's right. I'm not sure it's wrong either."

"Then write it and find out," Leane said, holding up a postcard of the Bastille. "Which one do you want?"

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Most news articles use the 'inverted pyramid': the most important facts come first and less important details follow, so the opening paragraph carries the core story.
story:
The radiator in Room 12B clanked like a small animal trapped in the wall, and Arianna had chosen the desk closest to it because the language lab was always cold, and because the cold gave her one more excuse to delay. On her worksheet lay a photocopied news article in her new language, forty lines of dense type about a river flooding a town, and at the bottom of the page her task, printed in cheerful bold: summarize aloud, in the new language, in ninety seconds. She had two days to prepare. She had already spent one of them sequestered in the library's far corner with a dictionary the size of a brick, and she had accomplished exactly one thing: she now knew the word for "moisture."

The trouble was where she had started. She had begun at the last paragraph, because in the novels she loved, the ending was where the truth lived, and it seemed judicious to save the beginning for later, when her vocabulary was stronger. But the last paragraph was a labyrinth: quotes from a woman whose roof had leaked, statistics about drainage, a sentence about the town's plans for next spring. Every clause demanded three trips to the dictionary. By closing time, she had translated four sentences and understood perhaps one, and the one she understood was about a municipal drainage committee, which she suspected was not the heart of anything.

"You look like the article bit you," said Adrien, sliding into the seat beside her the next morning. He smelled faintly of the cafeteria's orange juice, which he drank year-round, in all weathers, out of a dented metal bottle. He set his own worksheet on the desk. His article was about a football match.

"It's a flood," Arianna said. "Or a drainage committee. I genuinely cannot tell which is more important, and I have to say a summary out loud in front of everyone tomorrow."

Adrien turned her page upside down, considered it, and turned it back. "You started at the end, didn't you." It was not a question. He leaned over and tapped the first paragraph with two fingers. "Start here. My cousin edits a paper, she talks about it all the time. It's called the inverted pyramid. The most important facts come first, and the details after get less and less important. Your whole first paragraph is basically the core story." He shrugged, as if embarrassed to have said so much. "The last paragraph is probably like, what some guy thinks about the drainage."

Arianna looked at the first paragraph, which she had been avoiding the way you avoid the deep end of a pool. It was shorter than the others. When she worked through it, dictionary at her elbow, it opened like a door: the river had overflowed on Tuesday, two hundred residents had been evacuated, and the school had closed. Three facts. The flood, the people, the school. She sat back. She had spent an entire evening excavating the least important corner of the building while the entrance stood unlocked.

"Wait," she said slowly, "so the beginning is the summary. The article summarizes itself." This felt almost like cheating, and also almost like sophistry, some trick of arranging words so that reading became unnecessary, and she could not decide which it was. She read the second paragraph: roads closed, a shelter opened in the gymnasium. Also important. The third paragraph: an interview with the mayor. The fourth: the woman with the leaking roof, the drainage committee, the plans for next spring. The whole article lay in front of her like a staircase descending into detail, and she could stop wherever her ninety seconds ran out.

She practiced in the stairwell after class, where her voice bounced off the concrete and came back to her sounding braver than she felt. Isabela found her there, arms full of posters for the debate club, and stayed to listen, resting the posters against the railing. "Your word order is weird," Isabela said, "but I understood everything, and I understood it fast. Last week when you talked about your summer it took me three tries."

"The article did the work," Arianna admitted. "I just chose which parts to keep." She said it as a confession, but Isabela frowned at her like the confession was ridiculous. "Choosing is the work," Isabela said. "Anybody can read a paragraph out loud." She gathered her posters and clattered down the stairs, calling back that Arianna's pronunciation of "evacuated" had improved by at least forty percent, an estimate Arianna suspected had no basis in measurement.

In class the next morning, Ms. Kaur wrote the order of presenters on the board, and Arianna's name sat third, after a boy who read his summary flat off a paper he clearly could not have written himself, and a girl who spoke beautifully for two full minutes about the weather in her article before mentioning, in the final seconds, that the article was actually about a factory closing. Ms. Kaur thanked them both without comment, but her pen hovered over her clipboard in a way that suggested arithmetic.

When Arianna stood, the radiator clanked, and a boy in the back row whispered "the haunted heater" to his neighbor, and a laugh moved through the room like a small wave and broke against Ms. Kaur's raised eyebrow. Arianna folded her worksheet so only the first paragraph showed, though she barely needed it now. She said the river had overflowed on Tuesday. She said two hundred residents had been evacuated. She said the school had closed, and that a shelter had opened in the gymnasium, and that the mayor had promised the water would recede by the weekend, though she added, carefully, in the new language, "the article does not say if he is right." That last part was not in the article at all. It was hers, and she was not sure it belonged in a summary, and she said it anyway, because the residents in the gymnasium had faces she could imagine, and a promise about water seemed like the kind of thing a person should be allowed to doubt.

Ms. Kaur's pen moved for a long time on the clipboard. At the back, the radiator gave one more enormous clank, and Adrien raised his hand without waiting to be called on and said, "Can we get extra credit if the heater is actually haunted?"

activity: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
knowledge_domain: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
fact: Long or repeated exposure to sounds at or above 85 decibels can cause hearing loss, and the damaged hair cells in the human inner ear do not grow back.
story:
The appointment slip said 2:40, and Dominic had until 3:15, because Ms. Bondarenko locked the course-change drawer at 3:30 and the walk from the guidance office to the main office took eleven minutes if the hallways were clear. He had timed it yesterday. He sat now in the orange chair across from her desk, the form on his knee, the first box still empty, and the ringing in his left ear going on like a struck glass nobody would put a hand on.

"Audio engineering or the business program," Ms. Bondarenko said, reading his file without opening it. She already knew. "You put both down in September. The system kicks it back today."

"I know." The ringing had started Sunday night, after the show at the warehouse on Haldane, his sixth since June. It had faded a little by Tuesday, then come back Wednesday and stayed. He had not told anyone, not even Myah, who had been standing next to him at the front of the stage both nights they went in August.

He turned his phone over in his hands. On the screen was a decibel meter app he had downloaded in the parking lot this morning, before first period. In the cafeteria it had read 84, spiking to 90 when a tray dropped. At the warehouse on Sunday, if he was honest with himself, it would have pinned past that. He scrolled the app's info page again, the same paragraph he had read four times since homeroom: long or repeated exposure to sounds at or above 85 decibels can cause hearing loss. There was a second part he had not wanted to read twice, and he made himself read it now, in the waiting silence, the radiator ticking under the window behind Ms. Bondarenko's shoulder. The damaged hair cells in the human inner ear do not grow back.

"The registrar won't hold your spot in the studio cohort," Ms. Bondarenko said. "There are eleven kids on the waitlist. So this is a real deadline, Dominic, not one of the ones you ignore."

The door opened without a knock. Peyton, holding a guitar case by the neck like a lantern, her own form folded into a triangle in her fist. "Ms. B, I need a signature, quick, the band kids are all saying the drawer thing." She dropped into the chair beside Dominic, saw his screen, and leaned over. "Decibel app? You too?"

"My ears have been ringing since Sunday," he said. He had not meant to say it out loud, but in the small office, with the radiator ticking and Peyton's elbow an inch from his, the sentence transmuted from something he had been carrying privately into something that now belonged to the room.

"Mine ring after every gig," Peyton said. She said it lightly, the way people say things they have decided not to be afraid of. "Myah printed this thing off after the August show. Long or repeated exposure to sounds at or above 85 decibels can cause hearing loss, and the hair cells in your inner ear don't grow back. Ever." She shrugged. "I still don't wear plugs. Feels like a coward move, you know? Like you're admitting the music hurts you."

He looked at her. Something in how she said ever, flat and casual at once, landed harder than the paragraph had. "Peyton, that's the whole thing, though. It doesn't come back. That's not a feeling. That's just the structure of it."

Peyton's affective read of the situation, plugs equal cowardice, was a heuristic he had been running himself for two years: if it's loud, it matters; if it matters, you take it full volume. He could see now that the shortcut had been deciding for him. But he could also see the other direction people went, deciding everything was danger, and that felt like its own kind of lie. The truth he could stand on was narrower. He did not know if Sunday's ringing meant damage already done or just a warning. He did not know if audio engineering meant a life in exactly the rooms that had made his ears ring. What he knew was that the warning had a number, the number was 85, and the warning was not negotiable, because the cells did not regrow and no amount of caring about music would change that.

"I want the studio cohort," he said to Ms. Bondarenko. He uncapped his pen and wrote it in the first box, his handwriting smaller than usual. "But I'm going to need to do it differently than I've been doing."

"Differently how?"

"Plugs. Real ones, the flat-attenuation kind Myah was reading about, not foam. Measuring rooms before I mix in them. I don't know all of it yet." He signed his name at the bottom, and the clock above her filing cabinet said 3:01, and he pushed the form across the desk.

Ms. Bondarenko stamped it and held it a moment before handing it back. "Eleven minutes if the hallways are clear."

He stood. Peyton was still sitting, her folded form untouched in her fist, and she was looking at his phone where it lay face up on the chair, the meter running, the cafeteria noise outside her window reading 86.

"Dominic." She turned the form over and over in her fingers. "Where'd Myah say you get the real ones?"

"Music shop on Carlaw. I'm going there before it closes." He tucked the stamped form inside his jacket, where it could not be folded or lost. "Coming?"

Peyton stood, picked up the guitar case, and followed him out past the front desk, the form still creased in her hand.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: The Suzuki method, developed by Japanese violinist Shinichi Suzuki, teaches children to play by ear before reading music, the way they learn to speak before reading.
story:
David had wanted the guitar since he was fourteen, and now that he finally had one, secondhand and smelling of somebody else's attic, he discovered that wanting it for four years had taught him nothing about playing it. He sat on the edge of his bed with the chord chart his mother had printed from the library computer, pressing his fingertips until they creased white against the strings. The chart was precise, he'd give it that. Every chord had a diagram, every diagram had dots, and if he followed the dots exactly, he produced something that sounded like a door being closed on a cat.

On Saturday his neighbour's kid knocked, the nine-year-old from across the hall whose mother traded Ms. Yip for babysitting on alternating weekends. He had a small violin under his arm and an expression of professional patience. "My mom said you're learning an instrument," the boy said. "I've been learning for three years. Do you want to hear?" He did not wait for the answer, which David privately admired. He set the violin under his chin and played a folk tune David half recognized, clean and unhesitating, his small fingers finding the notes the way his own fingers found light switches in the dark.

David asked him to play it again, slower, and this time watched his eyes. They didn't move. The kid wasn't reading anything; there was no stand, no paper. He was reproducing sound from memory the way a person reproduces a sentence, without ever once consulting an alphabet. When David asked him to read the sheet music David had propped against his desk lamp, some beginner piano piece he'd found online, the boy squinted at it, turned it sideways, and admitted that notes on a page looked to him like flies on a wall. He could not read them at all.

"It's the Suzuki method," the boy said, as though this settled everything, and when David asked what that was, he shrugged. "Shinichi Suzuki. He was a Japanese violinist. You play by ear first, before you read music. Like how you learned to talk before you learned to read." He said it flatly, the way kids recite things they've heard a hundred times, and then he wanted to know if David's guitar could do anything louder.

After the boy left, David sat with the chord chart and tried to understand why the encounter had unsettled him. At school he had always been the one who trusted the diagram. In chemistry he'd copied procedures to the millilitre; in English he'd built essays sentence by sentence out of the teacher's rubric. If you gave David a system, he could operationalize it, break the goal into steps and climb them. That was the whole reason the chart had seemed like a promise when his mother printed it. But the kid across the hall had no chart and had never needed one, and somewhere in that there was a challenge David couldn't fit into a diagram.

He texted Amalia, who had played clarinet in the school band all four years and would have opinions. She came over with Phoenix, who had opinions about everything and credentials for almost none of them. They sat on his bedroom floor passing the guitar around badly. Amalia was a strong reader, she said, and a weak ear; in band she'd once transposed an entire piece rather than admit she couldn't hear that the key was wrong until the flute section told her. "So we're opposite," David said. "I could probably learn to read before I could play, and he learned to play before he could read." Phoenix suggested, as he suggested most things, that whichever way you were taught as a child was atavistic and inescapable, that David's generation of worksheet kids would produce worksheet adults forever. Amalia pointed out that Phoenix had said the same thing about handwriting in September and had since abandoned the position.

There was a version of this argument, David recognized, that could go on all night, each of them building a little casuistry out of anecdotes, matching every case to whatever conclusion they already preferred. He had done it himself in college application essays, weighing rigor against spontaneity and arriving, each time, at whichever value the prompt seemed to want. But sitting cross-legged on the floor with the guitar between his knees, he found he actually didn't know which way was better, or even whether better was the right question. Two routes to the same music, and he had only ever been shown one.

He put the chart in the drawer. Then he took it out and put it back on the desk, because that felt like a performance too, a gesture toward wildness he didn't honestly possess. Instead he asked Amalia to play the folk tune on her phone, the one the boy had played, and he listened to it four times with his eyes shut, trying to hold the shape of it in his head the way he held the shape of sentences. He found the first note on the fat string. It rang out over the fret, buzzed, and rang again.

Phoenix said it sounded like the door and the cat had reached an understanding. Amalia said do it again. David moved his finger one fret up and listened.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: In the UK, a driver who passes the test in an automatic car may drive only automatic cars, and must pass a manual test to drive a manual car.
story:
The car park behind the leisure centre smelled of cut grass and cold tarmac, and Olivia sat with her hands in her lap while Mr. Greco adjusted the mirror on her side. "Right," he said. "Feet on the pedals, no pushing yet, just feel where they are." She had chosen the manual lesson after three days of arguing with herself, mostly at the kitchen table while her mother drank tea and offered nothing. The family car was a manual, a pale blue hatchback with a gearstick worn shiny at the top, and it sat in the drive like a promise she hadn't yet earned the right to keep.

She had nearly rung the other school, the one with the cheerful automatics. Mahi had passed in an automatic back in spring and kept saying it was the sensible route, less to think about, quicker to test standard. "It's just easier," Mahi had said on the phone, and Olivia had agreed with her, and then hadn't booked it, and hadn't been able to say why. She distrusted decisions that arrived too easily, and she distrusted her own distrust, because sometimes easy was just easy and not a trap.

"Bite point," Mr. Greco said, once they'd rolled out onto the lane. "Find it. Slowly." The car bucked, coughed, died. A pheasant crossed the hedgerow gap ahead of them as if it had paid for the right of way. "Again," he said, without any change in his voice, and she pressed the clutch down and turned the key.

On the fourth attempt the engine caught and held, and the country road unspooled in front of them between hawthorn and wire fence, sheep regarding them from a slope like a jury that had already decided. She changed up to second, jerkily, and the whole machine shuddered and forgave her. Her father had said the car would teach her things an automatic never could, which she'd filed under Things Dads Say, but there was something in it she couldn't dismiss: the clutch made her feel the road as a set of decisions rather than a single continuous yes.

That evening, in the fish and chip queue with Jon, she said it out loud for the first time, trying the shape of the idea. "So if I pass my test in an automatic, that licence only covers automatics." She'd found it that afternoon, scrolling between lessons, and had read the line three times. "I'd have to pass a manual test as well before I could drive Mum's car." Jon, licking salt from his thumb, said, "Honestly, that might be the only argument that matters," and she laughed, but she knew it wasn't only that, and said so. The rule was real, but she hadn't chosen manual because of the rule; she'd found the rule afterwards and used it to reify a preference she'd already had, giving it edges and a name so it could stand up in an argument. She was honest enough with herself to find that slightly funny.

Second lesson, same road, rain now, the verges dark and glossy. Mr. Greco made her do hill starts on the long climb past the farm track, and she stalled six times, and each failure arrived with a small mechanical lurch that felt, briefly, like proof of something. In the college common room that week, arguing with Mahi again, Olivia had tried to describe why she liked the difficulty, and had reached for the word determinism and then pulled it back, because it wasn't right. The gearstick wasn't fate. It was more like a language, one where you had to conjugate the verbs yourself, and where mistakes were audible and correctable and yours.

The melancholic part, she admitted to herself somewhere in the third lesson, was the hatchback itself, which her grandfather had driven before it was theirs, and which would not last forever. Learning it felt like learning something with an expiry date already printed somewhere she couldn't read. She held that thought for a bend, then let the bend have her full attention, because that was the other thing the manual taught: it confiscated daydreams.

On the fifth lesson, a clear cold Thursday, she took the long straight past the paddocks in third, eased to fourth, and felt the change go in clean as a closing door. No lurch, no complaint, just the engine dropping its voice and the speedometer lifting. "There," said Mr. Greco. "That one, exactly that one." Sheep scattered at the sound of them, and the road bent left toward the village, and she went round it without stalling, down into the dip where the stream ran under the bridge.

She still didn't know whether she'd pass, or whether the easier route would have been wiser, or whether wisdom and ease were even the same currency. What she knew was the bite point under her left foot, the shape of the lane, and the fact of the hatchback waiting in the drive. "Same time next week?" Mr. Greco asked as they rolled back into the car park. Olivia pressed the clutch, found first, and said, "Book me in for the hill again."

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: In Ontario, a landlord may collect a rent deposit of no more than one month's rent, or one rent period if rent is paid more often, but may not charge a damage deposit.
story:
Anna spread the two leases across the kitchen table, one from a basement unit on Carling and one from a third-floor walk-up Samuel had found near the college. Her mother kept drifting past with a dish towel, pretending not to hover, and Anna pretended not to notice the pretending. The Carling lease looked cheaper at first glance, but she had learned enough in the past week to distrust first glances, so she made a third column in her notebook and began adding utilities, one lease at a time, into a single monthly total.

Tyson arrived before the kettle finished, letting himself in the way he had since they were eleven. He dropped into the chair across from her and pulled the walk-up lease toward him without asking, which was also the way he had done things since they were eleven. "This one says heat's included," he said. "That's like forty bucks a month right there."

"More like ninety in January," Anna said. "Hydro's separate on both. And the Carling one wants internet split with the upstairs tenant, which means I have to trust someone I've never met to pay half a bill on time."

Tyson tapped the page. "Then take the walk-up. Done. Can we eat something?"

She ignored him and kept working the arithmetic, because the arithmetic was the only part of this that behaved predictably. The walk-up came out to a total she could almost afford with the hours she had at the garden centre. The Carling place, even with heat included, did not, and that should have settled it. It didn't, because on the last page of the Carling lease there was a line about a deposit, and the number beside it was not one month's rent. It was one month's rent plus six hundred dollars, and the six hundred was labelled, in small confident print, "damage deposit."

Tyson saw her stop. "What?"

"Six hundred dollars extra," Anna said. "For damage. Is that a thing?"

"I don't know. People wreck places." He said it lightly, but he pulled the lease back and read the line himself, and Anna watched his easy certainty thin a little as he read it twice.

Down the hall, Ms. Mendoza, who had lived in the front apartment since before Anna's family moved in, was watering the ivy she kept on the windowsill by their shared landing. Anna's mother had gone out to her with a jar of soup an hour ago, and Anna now crossed the hall herself with the lease folded under her arm, because Ms. Mendoza had rented in three provinces and once, over coffee, had described a landlord of hers in terms so vitriolic that Anna's mother had laughed until she had to sit down. Ms. Mendoza listened to the question, set down her watering can, and did not lecture. She only said, "In Ontario, a landlord can take a rent deposit, but no more than one month's rent. And a damage deposit, they can't charge at all." Then she went back to her ivy, as if she had remarked on the weather, leaving Anna standing there with the whole fact rearranging the room around her.

From Ms. Mendoza's window the kitchen was visible, lit yellow, Tyson hunched over the papers with a stolen apple. He looked younger from out here, and also more serious, the way he got when something was wrong and he couldn't joke it flat. She thought of biology, third period, the unit Samuel actually paid attention to: mutualism, two organisms where both benefit, which is what a lease was supposed to be, tenant and landlord each gaining something from the other. The Carling lease was not that. It was one organism feeding on the other while calling it a contract.

Back in the kitchen, Tyson had written 670 on a napkin and circled it. "With the utilities and the internet," he said, "the walk-up's still more a month. You'd pay less every month at Carling if you could survive the deposit."

"If," Anna said. She sat down and pulled the notebook toward her, and beside her two columns she wrote a third: what each lease assumed about who she was. The walk-up assumed she had steady hours. Carling assumed she wouldn't check. She could tell the landlord what Ms. Mendoza had said and see what came back, or she could walk away and never learn whether he had known. Tyson watched her tap the pen against the page.

"Samuel's going to say take the cheap one," he said.

"Samuel isn't the one signing." She picked up her phone and began typing, asking if the damage deposit was a mistake or a policy, and while the message sat there unsent, Tyson got up without a word and put the kettle back on.

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: The derivative of a function at a point equals the slope of the line tangent to its graph at that point.
story:
The tutoring centre smelled of dry-erase marker and the orange pekoe that Mr. Abdi always left steeping too long, and Peyton had been staring at the same equation for eleven minutes. She wanted the scholarship exam passed in June, which meant calculus, which meant the recalcitrant little expression on the whiteboard had to stop being symbols and start meaning something. Bring down the exponent, subtract one. She could do the arithmetic. What she could not see was why anyone cared where the slope went to zero, or what a maximum had to do with a line that touched a curve only once.

Across the table, Gurshan was muttering at his own page. He was here for the English section, drilling his elocution for the interview portion, and he kept standing up mid-sentence to deliver his answers to the window as though the parking lot were an admissions panel. "I would say," he announced, "that my greatest weakness is perfectionism." He sat back down. "That's a lie, though. My greatest weakness is that I talk like a hostage."

"You talk fine," Peyton said, not looking up.

"I talk like someone subjugated by his own note cards. Mr. Abdi says I have to sound like I thought of it in the room." He tapped her paper with his pen. "Meanwhile you get to do math, which is just honesty with numbers."

Memphis arrived late, as always, hair still wet from swim practice, and dropped into the third chair with a box of cheese crackers he immediately offered around before taking any himself. He was in the math club, the actual competitive kind, and Peyton tolerated his presence because when she was stuck he had a way of asking one question too few. She slid her notebook toward him now without being asked, because she had learned that asking first only invited a lecture.

He studied it. On her graph paper she had plotted a curve, a simple upward-opening parabola flipped over, and beside it she had computed the derivative and set it equal to zero and found x, exactly as the textbook said. "You don't believe your own answer," Memphis said.

"I believe it. I just don't feel it."

He went to the supply shelf and came back with a wooden ruler. Without a word he laid it against her curve at the peak, dead level, the way a carpenter checks a shelf. "The derivative of a function at a point equals the slope of the line tangent to its graph at that point," he said, which was the kind of thing he said the way other people said hello. Then he tilted the ruler so it hugged the curve farther down the left side, steep and climbing. "So here, your derivative should be big. Check it."

Peyton substituted that x into her derivative and got a positive number, a large one, and something in her chest loosened. She moved the ruler to the right side of the curve, where the graph fell away, and computed a negative value there, the mirror of the first. At the top, the ruler lay flat, and her derivative gave zero, and the zero was not a trick anymore. It was the flat place. The maximum was just where the hill stopped rising before it started falling, which she had known about hills since she was four and had never once connected to algebra.

Mr. Abdi drifted over with his tea, looked at the ruler lying along her curve, and nodded once, the way he did when he decided not to intervene. But Gurshan was watching too, and he had his own want, and Peyton noticed it in the way he kept half-rising from his chair. "Could I try that?" he said. "Not the math. The ruler. If I can explain your hill out loud, clearly, no note cards, then I can explain anything."

She handed it over. Gurshan stood, laid the ruler against the rising side, and delivered it like a man reading weather to a village: "The slope here is steep and positive. Here it flattens. Here it is negative. The maximum is where it turns." He paused. "That was the best sentence I've said all month."

Memphis took a cracker and pointed it at Peyton. "So now do an ugly one. Cubic. Two turning points, and you have to test both."

Peyton wiped the board with her sleeve and started a new function, a cubic with coefficients she chose badly on purpose, and as she brought down the exponents she was honest with herself about what still hung loose: she understood the flat place and the falling place, but if someone asked her why the textbook called one turning point a maximum and the other only local, she would have to lay the ruler down again and find out. She wrote the derivative at the bottom of the board and set it equal to zero.

"Hand me the ruler," she said.

activity: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
knowledge_domain: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
fact: The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, set up in 1988 by the World Meteorological Organization and the UN Environment Programme, does no original research; it assesses the published scientific literature.
story:
Cohen had forty minutes before the debate team van left, and the argument he had built for the affirmative was falling apart on the table in front of him. His case rested on the claim that the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, the IPCC, had conducted experiments proving human-driven warming, and Umar had just leaned across the library table and said, with terrible confidence, "They run their own studies. Satellites, ice cores, all of it. That's why their reports are the gold standard." Cohen had nodded at the time, in the hallway that morning, because Umar's certainty always sounded like research. Now, alone among the study carrels, he wasn't so sure, and being unsure with a debate in forty minutes felt like standing on ice that had begun to tick.

He did what his mother called his worst habit and his best one: he went looking. The library's science section was two short shelves near the window, and the afternoon light lay across the spines in long pale bars. Mr. Popescu was reshelving at the far end, a cart of returns beside him, and he watched Cohen pull down volume after volume without comment. Cohen found a thin government pamphlet, a textbook with a cracked spine, and finally a fat blue book with IPCC in silver letters. He carried all three to a table by the radiator and started skimming for the sentence that would settle Umar's claim, one way or the other.

The blue book was not what he expected. There were no graphs from instruments the panel had built, no field stations, no expedition logs. Instead there were thousands of citations, page after page of them, studies carried out by other people in other countries, gathered and weighed and described. He flipped to the preface and read a paragraph twice, then a third time, because the words refused to arrange themselves into anything Umar had said. The panel, established in 1988 under the World Meteorological Organization and the UN Environment Programme, did no original research at all. It assessed the published literature. It read what everyone else had found.

"Missing something?" Mr. Popescu had come over with two books from the cart, and he set them down without looking at what Cohen was reading.

"The opposite," Cohen said. "I found something I wasn't looking for."

Mr. Popescu glanced at the blue cover, and something in his face shifted, the way a chess player's does when a beginner stumbles into a decent opening. "The index is in volume two," he said, and went back to his cart. That was all. Cohen sat with the book open and the radiator ticking under the window, and he began to understand that he had been building his argument on a picture of how science worked that he had never actually checked. He had imagined a single great laboratory issuing verdicts. What the book showed him was closer to a courtroom where the same case had been tried hundreds of times by different juries, and the panel was the clerk who read out what the verdicts had in common.

Umar arrived at twelve minutes to three, jacket half on, carrying the outline they were supposed to merge. "Tell me you've got the studies," he said, dropping into the chair across from Cohen. "The IPCC experiments. That's our strongest card."

"They don't do experiments," Cohen said.

Umar's face did the thing faces do when a load-bearing wall is removed. "Then what is it? What have they been doing for thirty years?"

"Reading," Cohen said, and turned the preface toward him. "They were set up in 1988, by the World Meteorological Organization and the UN Environment Programme, and they do no original research. They assess the published literature. That's the whole job. Other people do the studies, and other people check the studies, and then the panel reads all of it and says what it adds up to."

Umar read the paragraph himself, mouthing part of it, and Cohen watched his confidence drain and refill with something more careful. "So when Darius stands up and says it's just one organization's opinion," Umar said slowly, "it's actually the opposite. It's everybody's opinion. It's hundreds of separate results that kept saying the same thing."

"Which is a harder argument to attack," Cohen said, "and a harder one to make quickly." He pulled a blank sheet toward him and started rewriting the second section, and for a few minutes the two of them worked in the kind of silence that only happens when an idea is being taken apart and reassembled. Cohen kept one honest worry open at the back of his mind, the way you keep a window cracked: he still couldn't say exactly how the panel decided which studies deserved more weight, and if Darius asked him that, he'd have to admit it. He wrote in the margin, "Don't claim more than the book claims," a note to himself more than to the outline.

Darius came through the front doors at three sharp with his own binder under his arm, and the three of them walked out together toward the van. On the library steps Darius, who argued the negative and had clearly spent his lunch hour preparing, said, "I'm ready for you two. I've got a study from 2009 that says the whole thing is overstated, printed it out and everything."

Cohen felt the parsimonious shape of his new argument settle into place, all that sagacity the blue book had lent him, one careful claim underwritten by a hundred separate papers, and he almost smiled. "One study," he said, holding the door for Umar.

"One study is all I need," Darius said, and waved the printout like a ticket.

activity: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
knowledge_domain: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
fact: A 1990 follow-up of Mischel's preschoolers found that those who had waited longer for the second treat tended to have higher SAT scores as teenagers.
story:
Laurence had intended to spend the free period finishing her application for the summer research program, the one Mr. Gauthier had agreed to sign if she got it to him by three o'clock. Instead she was watching him set a jar of lemon candies on the front desk and announce, with the gravity of a man unveiling a monument, that anyone who did not take one until Friday would get two. He then left the room, presumably to see whether sixteen-year-olds were more patient than four-year-olds, or possibly just to get coffee.

Chace took one immediately, unwrapped it, and held it up like evidence. "Two on Friday is a lie invented by people who own jars," he said. He had been trying all week to recruit buyers for a console game he'd outgrown, and the candy fit somehow into his campaign of small immediate gains. He offered Laurence a half now if she promised to help him write the listing later, which was not a good trade, and he knew it, and offered it anyway.

Priya didn't take one either, but she took out her phone and started reading, and after a minute she looked up with the expression she wore when a fact had personally offended her. "Okay, so this is a real thing. Mischel. The preschoolers and the treats. In 1990 they followed up on the kids, and the ones who had waited longer for the second treat tended to have higher SAT scores as teenagers." She said it flatly, like a weather report, and then added, "Which is either amazing or completely unfair."

Laurence wrote the deadline for the program on the corner of her notebook and then, without deciding to, wrote "1990" under it. The application wanted five hundred words on a time she'd delayed gratification, which she'd been planning to invent something for, since her actual life consisted mostly of instant gratification punctuated by panic. Now she had a real incident, happening in real time, and she sat very still in her chair and felt the strange weight of it. One afternoon, one candy, and apparently the wiring for everything after. She was aware of how ridiculous that was. She was also aware that she was not eating the candy.

The problem was Chace, whose restlessness was mercurial enough to destabilize any room he occupied; he had now recruited two boys from the back row into a plan to sell the candy at lunch, on the theory that waiting was for people with trust funds. He kept drifting past her desk. He wanted her to say something, either to agree with him or to argue, because both were a kind of company. She had known him since grade eight and knew that his actual want, under the sales pitch, was the money for a bus pass his mother kept forgetting to renew, though he would rather have died than arrange the words in that order.

"You know the study followed them for years," she said. "The waiting showed up in 1990. SAT scores. Teenagers." She kept it short, the way Priya had said it, because the moment she made it a lecture she would sound like Mr. Gauthier, and Chace would eat the candy out of spite.

Chace considered the jar. "So the kids who waited got better scores. Fine. But the study can't tell you if they waited because they were smart, or if they were smart because they waited." He tapped the glass. "That's the part nobody puts on the poster." It was, Laurence had to admit, a genuinely good point, delivered by a boy attempting to sell a slightly scratched game console for thirty dollars.

She changed her mind twice in the next ten minutes. First she decided to wait, for the two candies and for the essay and for whatever distant SAT-shaped version of herself was supposedly watching. Then Priya mentioned that the program deadline was actually rolling, not fixed, that Mr. Gauthier had said so in September, and the whole architecture of the afternoon wavered. If the deadline was an illusion, was the waiting also an illusion, or was the waiting the only real thing in the room? Laurence put her pen down. Deterrence, she thought, works even when it's accidental; the candy sat there deterring nobody and everybody at once.

When the bell rang, the jar still held all but five candies. Chace had one in his mouth and was writing "LIKE NEW" on a slip of paper. Priya had found a second study on her phone and was frowning at it. Laurence closed her notebook with the deadline question unresolved and the essay unwritten, and picked up the jar to move it out of Chace's reach, and noticed that her hand was steady, and that nobody, not even the 1990 researchers, had ever measured that.

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: For ideal parallel plates, the field also equals the charge per unit area on a plate divided by the permittivity of free space, about 8.85 × 10^-12 farads per metre.
story:
The lab smelled of pencil shavings and the faint vinegar of old dry-erase markers, and the overhead projector, obsolescent now that every other room had a screen, rattled its fan in the corner like something breathing. Emilie sat on the high stool nearest the window, where the October light fell across her worksheet and made the paper nearly white against the grey counter. At the front of the room, Ms. Levy had drawn two long parallel lines on the board, pluses crowding the top line, minuses the bottom, and between them a single point marked with an arrow. "Field strength at P," she had said, tapping the point with the marker, "that's your job for the period."

Emilie read the problem a third time. Charge on each plate, given as 4.5 × 10⁻⁹ coulombs spread over an area of 0.090 square metres. Separation, 2.0 centimetres. And that was all. Every formula she knew for the field between plates wanted a voltage; she had copied E equals V over d into her notes only last week, underlined twice, and now it sat there useless, one letter short of a solution. Around her, pens scratched. Annabella, two stools over, kept glancing at the board as though the missing number might materialise among the pluses.

"Is the voltage somewhere?" Arian asked from the back, and half the class turned toward Ms. Levy, who only folded her arms and said, "No."

Annabella slid off her stool and drifted to Emilie's side, the way she did when a problem stopped being a problem and became a puzzle, which for her was the interesting kind. She had spent the summer reading philosophy forums and liked to say that physics had an ontology all its own, real things under the symbols, and that if you couldn't see the thing itself you were only transliterating it, copying letters from one language into another. Emilie had argued with her about it once on the bus, but she thought of it now, because staring at the worksheet was giving her nothing but letters.

She flipped back through her notes, past the day on Coulomb's law, past a sketch of a single charged sphere. Somewhere, she half remembered, there had been a different route. She found it on a page from a chapter they hadn't been assigned: a boxed line saying the field between ideal parallel plates also equalled the charge per unit area on a plate divided by the permittivity of free space, which the book put at about 8.85 × 10⁻¹² farads per metre. She read it twice, then said the phrase out loud, quietly, just to hear it whole: "permittivity of free space."

Annabella leaned over her shoulder. "So you don't need the voltage at all?"

"Charge per area, then divide by that constant." Emilie wrote it out. 4.5 × 10⁻⁹ divided by 0.090 gave 5.0 × 10⁻⁸ coulombs per square metre. She divided that by 8.85 × 10⁻¹², working carefully, checking each exponent, and got something near 5,650 newtons per coulomb. The arithmetic had a clean, unarguable feeling, the way long division had in primary school, but she distrusted the feeling. Numbers that felt clean had fooled her before.

She was still hovering over it when the bell for break rattled and most of the class drained into the corridor, Arian carrying the projector's complaint to the door with him, complaining that the machine belonged in a museum. Ms. Levy stayed at her desk, and Emilie noticed her watching the two of them without impatience, the way you watch bread rise. Annabella pulled the second stool closer and nudged Emilie's calculator. "Do it backward," she said. "If your field's right, what voltage would it need?"

Emilie multiplied by the separation, 0.020 metres, and got 113 volts. Which meant nothing to her, still just letters and units, a transliteration of a thing she couldn't see. She was about to say so when Ms. Levy came over with the whiteboard eraser in her hand and a smear of blue ink on her cuff, and Emilie saw, for the first time, a faint ghost on the board itself: the shape of a digit half rubbed out between the two drawn plates, where someone, hours earlier, must have wiped a number away without noticing. The 113 matched what had been written there before it was erased, and Ms. Levy confirmed it with one raised eyebrow and said, "That's why no voltage on your sheet. I didn't need to give you one."

The bell rang again, and the class came back in a wave of cold air and wet coats, Arian among them, shaking rain off his sleeve and apologising, because it turned out he had been the one at the board during lunch duty, wiping it down too thoroughly with a paper towel. Annabella laughed, and Emilie found she was laughing too, though what stayed with her was stranger than that. She had reached the field from two directions, charge and voltage, and the two had agreed, and yet she could not have said which one was the real thing under the symbols, or whether there was a real thing there at all. She copied the erased digit back onto the board beside her answer, nice and dark, so the next class would have it, and stood a moment with the marker uncapped in her hand.

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: In Java, a field marked private can be read or changed only by code inside the same class.
story:
Aidan had agreed to come to Elizabeth's basement mostly for the air conditioning, but he stayed because her brother's old laptop had a sticker on it that said THINK, and he felt that a machine making a demand like that deserved company. The assignment on the screen was due Monday: build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods, then test it. Ms. Horváth had written it on the board in her tidy capitals, and Aidan had copied it down without understanding a word, which was his usual relationship to board work.

Elizabeth wanted hers done by eight, because a boy named after a saint was coming over at nine, and she had made it clear that a half-finished program was the kind of thing that could follow a person around. Clovis sat cross-legged on the carpet with his own laptop, allegedly doing the same assignment, actually watching a video about a politician who, according to the narrator, was a demagogue of the first order. Clovis liked the word so much he said it out loud twice.

"Private," Aidan read from the assignment sheet. "Fields. Getters." He typed a class called Book with a field for the title and set it to private, because the sheet said to, the way he fastened his seatbelt: not from conviction but from a general policy of compliance.

Then he wrote the test. He made a Book, gave it a title, and asked the test to print the title, directly, plainly, like reaching into a box. He pressed run.

The compiler refused. It underlined one line in red and produced a message saying the field was not visible, and Aidan stared at it with the particular resentment of a person who has been told the door is locked after pushing on it. "I made the thing," he said. "It's mine. It's in the same file."

Elizabeth leaned over, chewing the cap of a pen she would later lose between the couch cushions. "Wait, go back," she said. "Read the red part again."

He read it again. The field was private, the test could not touch it, and the class itself, apparently, could. He sat with that for a second, chin on his fist. So the private field could be read or changed only by code inside the same class, and the test lived outside, in a different class entirely, close enough to see but not to touch. "It's like the field has a bank vault around it," he said, "and the test is standing outside with its face against the glass."

"That's the getter," Elizabeth said, already typing her own version, because she was the kind of person who wanted to seem fluent more than she wanted to be careful. "You make a method inside the class that hands the value out through the little slot."

Aidan built the getter, a small method that returned the title, and the test compiled and printed the title and glowed with the modest triumph of a lightbulb. But then he paused, cursor blinking, and thought about it honestly, which he did sometimes when nobody was watching. Two ideas were arguing in him. His old idea said restrictions on your own property were insults; the compiler's idea said a wall was not a wall against you but a wall for you, a way of deciding exactly what got in. He was not sure yet which idea he actually held, or whether the truth was some turbid mixture of both, and he suspected the assignment would be graded before he found out.

"Why would anyone valorize the wall, though," Clovis said from the carpet, not looking up. "You put the data in, you should get the data out."

"You'd think," Aidan said. He looked at Elizabeth's screen, where her class had a private field and a getter and, he noticed, no way at all to change the field once it was set, which was either a mistake or a philosophy. "Yours doesn't have a setter."

Elizabeth checked the clock, which said 7:40, and hit run. The doorbell rang at nine on the dot, and from the top of the stairs they heard her take the stairs two at a time.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: Hydroplaning happens when a layer of water builds up between the tires and the road so the car loses traction; easing off the accelerator can let the tires regain grip.
story:
The licensing office smelled of wet coats and burnt coffee, and Matthew waited in line behind a man arguing about an expired tag with the patience of someone who had argued about it before. His mother had dropped him at the curb with the kind of hug that suggested driving was a ceremony of leaving, which was not how Matthew thought of it. He thought of it as a certificate he needed for the job at the warehouse, where the pay was enough that he could stop asking her for grocery money, a small private insolvency he intended to end without announcing it. When his number came up, the clerk slid a laminated sheet across the counter and said his instructor would be Mr. Haddad, and that the road test would be scheduled once the hours were logged.

Mr. Haddad was waiting outside in a dented sedan with a second steering wheel bolted on the passenger side, though Matthew noticed it did not actually connect to anything. "You have driven nothing?" Mr. Haddad asked, and Matthew admitted to a riding mower, a boat once, and a golf cart he and Francisco had taken across a fairway at two in the morning. Mr. Haddad absorbed this without visible judgment and told him to adjust the mirrors until he could see the rear tires, because the rear tires were where a car kept its honesty.

The first hour was parking lots. Matthew stalled twice, over-corrected constantly, and discovered that the steering wheel wanted to be moved in small amounts rather than the dramatic rotations he had seen in movies. Mr. Haddad spoke in short instructions and long silences, reticent in a way that Matthew eventually understood was deliberate, a space left open for the student to fill with his own mistakes. When Matthew asked whether they would go on an actual road, Mr. Haddad looked at the sky, where the clouds had been thickening all afternoon, and said, "Roads are wetter when it rains."

They pulled out onto the county road at dusk, wipers slapping, and Matthew drove with his hands at ten and two the way the booklet had said, though the booklet had not mentioned how the rain reduced everything to gray shapes and guessing. He liked it anyway. The speedometer needle sat at forty, the headlights tunneled into the rain, and he felt a competence he could not yet justify. Behind them a truck flashed its lights, and Mr. Haddad told him to pull forward, which Matthew did, accelerating gently past a stretch where the pavement dipped and water had gathered in a long dark sheet.

The steering went light. It was the strangest sensation, as if the car had been picked up by its collar and carried. The wheel turned freely in his hands and nothing happened, the road continuing to curve while the car did not curve with it, and Matthew heard himself make a small sound he would later decline to describe to Francisco. His whole body wanted to brake, wanted to stamp on the pedal and take control, because that was what you did when things slipped, you grabbed.

"Off the gas," Mr. Haddad said, quietly, almost bored.

Matthew eased his foot off the accelerator. For a second, nothing, the car still floating on the water, and then the tires found the road again with a shudder and the steering went heavy and true, and the curve unspooled ahead of them exactly as it was supposed to. His heart was going like a bird against a window. "What was that," he said, not really a question.

"It's called hydroplaning," Mr. Haddad said. "Water builds up between the tires and the road, and you lose traction. You ease off, the tires find their grip again." He said it the way he said everything, as though reporting on weather in another country. Matthew drove the next mile in silence, feeling the shape of it in his mind. His instinct had been to seize control, and the correct move had been to release it, to trust the machine to find its own way back down to the road. He thought about his mother, who handled every crisis by grabbing it with both hands, and about Francisco, who handled crises by not noticing them, and he suspected, without being able to prove it, that the truth lived somewhere between, that there were moments for gripping and moments for letting go, and that knowing which was which was the actual skill, the thing no laminated sheet could certify.

They pulled back into the lot at full dark. Mr. Haddad wrote something on his clipboard and slid it across the seat for a signature, and Matthew saw the word "satisfactory" and the number of hours logged, one of ten. "Next week, highway," Mr. Haddad said, unbuckling. Matthew signed, then sat for a moment with his hands still on the wheel, ten and two, before handing over the keys.

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
knowledge_domain: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
fact: In a minor-key sonata-form movement, the exposition's second theme usually moves to the relative major, such as E-flat major in a movement in C minor.
story:
Liam sat at his grandfather's upright piano with a photocopied score of the Mozart sonata K. 457 spread across the music rack, a pencil behind his ear, and a deadline ticking in his head: Mr. Szabó wanted the analysis marked up by Monday, first theme, second theme, closing, development, recapitulation, all bracketed in the margins. The house smelled of coffee and old paper. Rain worked at the windows. He had been at it for two hours and the exposition was still refusing to break cleanly in half.

The first theme was easy. It arrived in the first bar like a fist on a table, C minor, loud, ornamented, unmistakable. The closing section was easy too, all those running figures piling up at the end of the exposition. The trouble sat in the middle, in the second theme, which began somewhere around bar forty-one and did something he had not expected. He had a theory paper's worth of rules in his head, and one of them said a second theme should move to the dominant, should establish it, prepare the return. He had even written a small G in the margin, circled it, twice.

He played the passage. The right hand sang something almost tender over a rolling left hand, and it did not sound like G minor or G anything. It sounded, for want of a better word, relieved. He played it again, slower, and hummed the bass down to its floor.

His grandfather came in with two mugs and set one on the far end of the table, away from the score, a man who had spilled tea on a first edition once and never forgiven himself. "Still on the Mozart?"

"Still on the second theme," Liam said. "It's not doing what it's supposed to do."

"Nothing by Mozart ever does," his grandfather said, and went back to the kitchen, and Liam thought about texting Kelly-Anne, who had already finished her analysis of a different sonata and had offered, with unbearable cheer, to send him a photo of her markings. He had said no. He wanted, though he could not have said why until later, to find the answer in the notes and not in her photograph, the same way he wanted to understand why Daria had stopped sitting with him at lunch, which was a question no one could hand him the answer to either.

He played the passage a third time and let his ear lead instead of his theory. The bass settled on E-flat. He stopped, lifted his hands, and stared at the circled G in the margin like it was a malevolent little prophecy. E-flat. The key sat three flats away from C minor in the signature, close kin, and the more he played the theme the more it made a strange kind of sense: after all that darkness in the opening, the music had turned to the relative major, E-flat major in a movement in C minor, not to the dominant at all. He erased the G slowly, the rubber smearing graphite across the stave, and wrote E-flat instead, then sat with his hand flat on the page as though the pencil might try to change its mind.

The phone buzzed against the piano lid. Daria, of all people. He let it buzz out. He did not want to resuscitate that conversation, not here, not with the score half-solved and his grandfather moving dishes in the next room. He turned back to the page and found the double bar, the exposition's end, and then the development, where Mozart took his two themes and dismantled them in the dark, and then, ten pages on, the recapitulation, where everything came home.
