The district office had seen a draft. There were concerns about tone. There were relationships to think about, partnerships, the district's relationship with the paper's printer, which was a company the board had a contract with. Nothing was threatened. Everything was implied.

"We could soften the second paragraph," Dimitrios said now, leaning back in the broken chair that listed to the left. He was eating sunflower seeds and spitting the hulls into an empty film canister, an old habit from his uncle's store. "Take out the board member's name. Keep the argument."

"Then it isn't the argument." Grace sat on the desk itself, heels tapping the cabinet below. The room smelled of toner and the oranges Johnny had left half peeled on the windowsill, going soft in the radiator heat. Outside, the parking lot was emptying bus by bus, the late bus among them for now, its yellow flank sliding past the window like evidence.

Johnny came in with his camera and the smell of cold air on his jacket. "Two juniors cried in the front office today," he said. "Turned out the late bus was the only way they got home after robotics. The secretary gave them bus fare out of her own purse."

"So we run it," Dimitrios said, but he said it to the ceiling.

Grace looked up at the curling page and remembered, suddenly and completely, a night in October of the previous year. She had been at her father's apartment, doing homework with the television on, and a news anchor had said that the Los Angeles Times had not endorsed a presidential candidate that October, after the paper's owner blocked the editorial board's plans. She remembered her father looking up from his laptop. "Members of the board resigned over it," he had said. "They walked out of their own paper." She had been sixteen and had thought it was a story about faraway people, adults in a tower, and she had gone back to her chemistry.

She thought about it now while Johnny ate one of his oranges and Dimitrios cracked another seed. The paper at her father's was owned by a man, and the man had wants, and the wants had shaped what the paper said, and the journalists had chosen between their bylines and their silence. It had seemed simple then, a morality play. It did not seem simple now. The principal had not blocked anything. He had only leaned, the way wind leans on a door.

"Here's what I keep turning over," she said slowly. "If we run it with the name and the district pulls the printing contract, the paper dies for a semester, maybe for good, and nobody covers anything again. If we soften it, we print something that looks like courage and isn't, and we learn to call that normal."

Dimitrios stopped spitting hulls. "That's the pugnacious version and the cowardly version, you mean."

"Neither," Grace said. "That's what I can't solve." She picked at the tape on the wall, pressing the corner back down with her thumb. "I want to be the person who resigns. But there's no one to resign to. It's my paper and it's theirs at the same time."

Johnny, who was the least dramatic of them and therefore often the most useful, set down his orange. "Run the editorial," he said. "And run the story of the secretary paying the bus fare, and the two juniors, with photos, on the front page. If they cut the contract, we print it on the school copier, folded and stapled, ugly. It'll look worse for them than for us."

Grace considered it. The scent of oranges sat between them like an offered thing. It was not the pure act she had wanted, and it was not surrender either; it was a compromise in the old sense, a promise both risky and shared, and she could not say for certain that it would hold. She thought of the resigning board members and wondered whether they had felt clean or merely free, and whether those were the same. She did not know. She suspected she would not know for years.

"Get me the photos by Friday," she said, and reached for the layout sheet, and the curling page above her settled, for the moment, flat.

activity: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
knowledge_domain: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
fact: The ancient Greek historian Thucydides admitted that the speeches in his history of the Peloponnesian War were not word-for-word records, but what he judged each speaker would have needed to say.
story:
The monument was a granite obelisk at the edge of the park, taller than the trees around it, and Thomas had walked past it every school day for four years without reading a single word of the inscription. That changed in October, when Mr. Mensah assigned the senior class a speech to be delivered at the Remembrance Day ceremony, and Thomas, to his own surprise, won the draft lottery that decided who would stand at the base of the obelisk and address the town.

He chose Pericles. He'd found the Funeral Oration in a battered anthology his mother kept from her own college days, and the language did something to him: "What I would prefer is that you should fix your eyes every day on the greatness of Athens as she really is." He copied out six lines on an index card and practiced them on the walk home, giving the sidewalk pigeons a performance they did not appear to appreciate.

Caleigh caught him at it near the monument itself, and she laughed so hard she had to sit on the bottom step of the obelisk. "You're doing the Pericles thing," she said. "Kaiden did that same speech for debate last year. He opened with the glory line and everything."

"Then he opened with the best part," Thomas said, and Kaiden, who had been trailing behind them with two coffees, jogged up to defend his honor.

"Except it's fake," Kaiden said. "Not fake, but. Ask Mensah. Or don't, because he'll make it a whole lesson. It's Thucydides. The guy who wrote the history of the Peloponnesian War. He admitted right at the start that the speeches in it weren't word-for-word records. He said he wrote what he judged each speaker would have needed to say."

Thomas felt the index card go strange in his pocket, as if it had shrunk. "Needed to say," he repeated. "So nobody knows what Pericles actually said. Not exactly."

"That's the fun part," Caleigh said. "Nobody knows. Welcome to actual history, it's all footnotes and arguing."

He went home and found it himself, which took longer than it should have, because first he spent forty minutes watching a documentary about shipwrecks as a form of avoidance. But there it was, in a translation of Thucydides, the historian stating plainly that keeping the speeches as they were actually given was impossible, and that he had rendered instead what each speaker ought to have said, in his own judgment, given the situation. Thomas read the paragraph three times. It was not a scandal. It was a confession, and somehow the confession made him trust the book more and his index card less.

The problem was practical. In four days he had to stand at the obelisk and speak about the town's dead, and his speech was built on six lines that were half Thucydides and half a dead Athenian, and he could no longer pretend otherwise. He tried drafting something original and produced two pages that sounded like a greeting card that had been left out in the rain. Kaiden read one page over his shoulder and said, kindly, "Delete that before it hurts somebody."

The night before the ceremony, Thomas walked back to the monument alone. He had rewritten the speech as an argument, and he was not sure it was tenable, and he was even less sure it was what a Remembrance Day crowd wanted. But standing there in the cold, reading it quietly to the obelisk, he found he liked it better than the borrowed grandeur. He had kept two of the Pericles lines. He had kept them knowing what they were.

On the day, the crowd was small and older than he'd expected, and a woman in a wool coat near the front held a photograph of a young man in uniform. Thomas spoke. He told them the lines he was about to read came to us through a historian who admitted he had composed the speeches himself, shaping what each speaker would have needed to say, and that this seemed to him honest in a way worth imitating, because the dead of this town also survive only in fragments, in what their families judged them to be, and we hand those on too. He could hear Mr. Mensah at the back, and he could hear a child somewhere asking, loudly, whether they could get chips after, and the woman with the photograph was crying, and Thomas could not tell whether he had given her something or taken something away. He finished the Pericles lines anyway, because they were beautiful, and because a town with a granite obelisk and no surviving dissident voices to contradict it deserved at least that.

Afterward, Caleigh found him by the steps. "That was either the best or the worst Remembrance Day speech this town has ever had," she said. "There's no middle option. Kaiden's already trying to commodify it, he wants you to do the debate banquet next month."

"Tell him no," Thomas said, and then, because the cold had made him honest, "Tell him maybe."

He folded the index card once and put it deep in his coat pocket, where he could feel its square corner against his hip all the way home.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: A food bank is usually a central warehouse that collects and distributes food to local agencies, while a food pantry is where people pick up food directly.
story:
Noah had signed up because the form said volunteers were needed at the food bank on Delmore Street, and he had imagined, on the walk over, a queue. Something like a soup kitchen with shelves, people carrying bags of rice out into the evening. What he found instead was a warehouse with a roller door and the smell of cardboard, and inside it a man named Mr. Mokoena directing a forklift like an orchestra conductor who had grown impatient with the strings.

"You're the school lot," Mr. Mokoena said, which was half true. Noah had come alone; Leonie and Jaden had arranged to meet him there, an arrangement that augured well for nobody's punctuality. Leonie arrived twelve minutes later with a camera, and Jaden arrived eighteen minutes after that holding a clipboard of his own, on which his volunteer hours were to be recorded, verified, and eventually converted into something a college admissions office would find moving.

The work was not what Noah had pictured either. Nobody came in for groceries. All morning they weighed pallets of tinned beans, checked dates, sorted dented cans into a bin labelled NOT FOR DISTRIBUTION, and loaded boxes into a white van belonging to something called the Riverbend Pantry. Noah kept glancing at the roller door in case a family wandered in looking for dinner, and nobody did, and after a while the silence where the queue should have been began to feel like a question he was too embarrassed to ask.

Leonie was taking photographs of the sorting table, crouching to get the light right. "This one's good," she said, showing him the screen: his own hands placing a can of chickpeas onto a pallet, the whole frame warm with dust. "I'm building a portfolio on labour. Documenting work nobody photographs." Jaden, meanwhile, had found a folding chair and was filling in his sheet in careful print, TIME IN, TIME OUT, leaving nothing blank that a supervisor might later initial. He wanted, he had told Noah on the walk from the bus stop, forty hours by spring, ideally without encountering forty hours of anything.

It was the van driver, back for a second load, who finally gave Noah the shape of the thing. He was a thin man from Riverbend who counted boxes aloud and joked about his knees, and when Noah asked him, apologetically, why nobody just came here, the driver looked at him without any judgement at all.

"This is the food bank," he said. "A food bank is the warehouse that collects the food and sends it out to the local agencies. The pantry is where people pick up the food directly. We're the pantry."

"Oh," Noah said. "So this is like the, what, the sedimentary layer underneath."

"Sure," the driver said, in the tone of a man who had decided not to pursue geology.

Noah found that the distinction rearranged the whole morning for him, and rearranged something in him too, though he was careful not to announce it. He had come expecting to hand a bag of groceries to a hungry person, to be, for two hours, visibly good. Instead the goodness was structural, layered, mostly invisible; his cans would travel in the van to Riverbend and be stacked there and eventually be carried out through a door he would never see, by hands that were not his. He could hold both pictures at once, the direct and the distributed, and he noticed that he did not entirely know which one was more generous, or whether that was even the right question. He kept sorting either way, because the pallet did not care about his uncertainty, and neither did the driver's knees.

At four o'clock Jaden presented his clipboard to Mr. Mokoena with the ceremony of a boy submitting a treaty. Mr. Mokoena read it slowly, and then read it again, and then looked up over the top of it.

"Forty hours, you want," he said. "Good. I need someone every Saturday, ten to two. Sorting, then riding along to Riverbend, then unloading at the pantry where the actual people are. You'll see more than you bargained for." He clicked his own pen and signed the first day's line. "I'll expect you."

Jaden looked at the signature, then at the van, then at his own carefully blank schedule. Leonie was already photographing his face.

"I'll need to check some dates," Jaden said faintly.

"Check them fast," said Mr. Mokoena, and handed him a second clipboard.

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: High blood pressure often causes no symptoms at all, which is why it is called a silent killer and is found mainly by measuring it.
story:
Dominic stood in his grandfather's cramped bathroom, the upper arm cuff humming as it tightened, the digital display blinking up a pair of numbers he had only ever seen in the pamphlet from Ms. Doyle's health class. 148 over 94. He copied it into his notebook beside the earlier readings, 122 over 78 from the gym last Tuesday and 136 over 88 from Thursday, and then just looked at them, because looking was easier than deciding what they meant.

The assignment had seemed simple a week ago. Ms. Doyle wanted each of them to learn a measurement they'd never done before and present it: interpret one reading, then explain how diet and exercise could change it. Corbin had chosen skinfold calipers, mostly as an excuse to pinch Cayden's arm during lunch, and Cayden had retaliated by choosing resting heart rate and taking his own pulse dramatically during every class. Dominic had picked blood pressure because nobody else had, and because his grandfather owned a monitor, bought after a hospital visit nobody in the family discussed directly.

"You hiding in there?" his grandfather called through the door.

"No, I'm working. Measuring you, remember?"

"Measure away. I feel fine, so it'll be fine."

Dominic unlatched the door. His grandfather was leaning in the hallway in his cardigan, seventy-one and vain about his walks, the kind of man who considered illness a failure of manners. He came in and sat on the edge of the tub, because there was nowhere else, and held out his arm.

The bathroom was the one room in the house where everything got said plainly. Dominic had figured this out years ago, after his grandmother died, when he'd found his mother crying at the sink with the tap running to cover the sound. A flashback surfaced now, unbidden: he was eleven, sitting on the closed toilet lid while his grandfather shaved, and his grandmother called through the door that her head ached, and his grandfather said, "You and your headaches," and they had both laughed, and ten months later she was gone. Dominic hadn't thought about that morning in years. He thought about it now while the cuff inflated and his grandfather winced at the squeeze.

"142 over 92," Dominic read.

"Mean anything?"

"It's high. You're above the normal range." He turned the notebook toward his grandfather. "It was high Thursday too. Both readings I took."

His grandfather waved a hand, as if dismissing a waiter. "I'd know if something were wrong. I feel fine."

Dominic hesitated. This was the part Ms. Doyle hadn't taught him directly; he'd found it at midnight on his phone, screen dimmed under his blanket, while his mother watched television downstairs. He'd assumed the fact would be complicated, but it was one sentence, and it had changed the shape of the whole assignment. "That's the thing," he said. "High blood pressure often causes no symptoms at all. That's why they call it a silent killer. It gets found by measuring it, mostly. Not by how you feel."

His grandfather was quiet for a moment, rubbing his arm where the cuff had left a crease. Then he said, "Your grandmother felt fine."

Dominic hadn't expected that. He didn't know what the doctors had said about his grandmother, whether pressure had been part of it, and he understood suddenly that he might never know, because the family had conducted its own quiet casuistry around her death, reasoning each symptom into something smaller, each headache into a long day, each fatigue into the weather. He had done it too. He remembered telling himself she was just tired.

"The project," he said carefully, "is about how diet and exercise change it. Salt especially. And regular aerobic stuff, like your walks, but more of them." He tapped the notebook. "You'd have to do it for weeks before the numbers moved. That's the honest part. One reading means almost nothing."

"So you're saying measure me again."

"I'm saying let me measure you again. Next weekend, and after that." He paused. "And maybe don't salt the tomatoes tonight."

His grandfather laughed, a short seismic sound in the small tiled room, and stood up. "You sound like your mother. She's been trying to get me to walk after dinner for a year." He looked at himself in the mirror over the sink, adjusted the cardigan, and Dominic realized that his grandfather wanted something too, though it wasn't the same thing Dominic wanted. His grandfather wanted to be the man who was fine, the man who didn't need the cuff or the notebook or the grandson taking readings in his bathroom, and admitting the numbers were high would cost him that. Whereas Dominic wanted, more than he could quite say aloud, to have caught something early this time, to have measured instead of assumed, to asuage a guilt he hadn't known he was carrying until this week.

At the front door, later, his grandfather pressed a paper bag of tomatoes into his hands. "Salt's in the bag," he said. "Separate."

Dominic laughed and carried the tomatoes out to his bike, the notebook zipped into his backpack with 142 over 92 written twice, once in ink and once, fainter, where his pen had gone through the page.

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
knowledge_domain: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
fact: In a LEFT JOIN, putting a condition on the right table in the WHERE clause, like orders.total > 0, removes the NULL rows and makes it act like an inner join.
story:
Brandon had been at Braylon's kitchen table for forty minutes, and the laptop screen still showed the same eleven rows. "That's not right," he said. "There are supposed to be more."

Braylon leaned over from his side of the table, chair legs squeaking on the tile. "Eleven seems like a lot of customers."

"No, it's eleven customers who ordered something. Mr. Sutherland wants the ones who ordered nothing. That's the whole assignment." Brandon scrolled up to his query, a LEFT JOIN between the customers table and the orders table, and pointed at the WHERE clause he'd added ten minutes ago. "It worked before I put that in. It gave me forty rows, and most of them had NULL in the order column, which is what nothing looks like."

"NULL," Braylon said, peevish now, because he'd been trying to watch a video on his phone and kept getting pulled into a subject he didn't take. "Why can't nothing just be a zero? Who decided empty gets its own special word?"

Lauryn, who had been quiet at the counter making herself tea, carried her mug over and sat down. She wanted the kitchen to feel like a study hall again, the way it had last semester before Brandon dropped out of their study group for reasons he never explained and she never asked about. She was not going to let this afternoon end with Braylon retreating to his room. "Run it both ways," she said. "Take the filter out, run it, put it back, run it again. Then you'll know which piece is lying to you."

That was how Brandon learned to stop guessing, though he wouldn't have said it that way. He deleted the condition on the orders table, ran the query, and counted forty rows, most of them customers whose order columns sat empty. He typed the condition back in, exactly as before, a filter on orders.total, and the list collapsed to eleven again, every remaining row a customer with a real order. He sat back. "It's the filter. The filter is what's deleting them."

Lauryn pulled the laptop closer and read the line aloud, slow, like proofreading an essay. "So when you put a condition on the right table in the WHERE clause, it throws out the NULL rows." Brandon nodded, and something assembled itself in his mind out of the pieces: two kinds of join, one that kept the empty side and one that didn't, and his filter quietly turning the first kind into the second. He rewrote the query, moving the condition out of WHERE, and when he ran it this time the list came back long, with the nothing-orderers at the bottom, forty rows, the quiet customers surfacing at last. "It acts like an inner join," he said, mostly to himself. "That's what it was doing the whole time."

Mr. Sutherland had told them once that a database was a set of promises about the world, and Brandon thought about that now, about how a person could write a true condition and still end up lying, because truth in one clause became untruth in another. But he also knew he was guessing about the part he'd moved, and he said so. "I don't fully get why the other spot works," he admitted. "I just know it does."

"That's fine," Lauryn said. "Write it down anyway." She slid a napkin across the table, and Braylon, who had put his phone face down without anyone asking him to, found a pen in the junk drawer and set it beside the napkin. Brandon copied the two versions of the query onto the paper, one labeled broken, one labeled not, the ink bleeding a little where the napkin was thin.

Later, when Lauryn was rinsing her mug and Braylon had finally gone back to his video with the sound low, Brandon folded the napkin into his pocket. He paused at the counter beside her. "Next week, same table?" he asked. "I owe you one." Lauryn looked at him for a second, then at the chair she'd claimed, the one with the good afternoon light. "Bring your own tea," she said, and turned off the faucet.

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: Signalling before a merge or lane change warns other drivers of the move; signalling too late, or not at all, gives them no time to adjust.
story:
The laundromat on Fenwick Street had a battered sofa, a change machine that ate quarters, and a back wall of fogged windows, which meant Gabrielle could watch the parking spots across the road while the dryers tumbled. She had been coming here every Thursday since her mother declared the household's patience with driving lessons officially exhausted. Thursdays were also when Ms. Bui, who owned the laundromat and lived above it, set out a lawn chair by the door and graded the parking of anyone foolish enough to attempt the curb across the street.

"You're back," Ms. Bui said, not looking up from her crossword.

"Test's on the sixteenth," Gabrielle said. She fed quarters into the washer and thought about how to say the rest. "I can do everything except the two things they actually fail you on."

"Parallel parking," Ms. Bui said, "and merging." She pencilled in a word, studied it, erased it. "The usual martyrs."

Cierra and Tayla arrived at four with a laundry bag that clinked and a paper tray of fries they had no intention of sharing. They had passed their tests the previous spring, in the profligate way of people for whom things come easily, and ever since they had been conducting a low campaign of commentary on Gabrielle's behalf. "You could practise on our street," Tayla offered, mouth full. "Nobody parks on our street. Nobody drives on our street. A deer could parallel park on our street."

"That's the problem," Gabrielle said. "There's nothing to park between."

Between the two of them, though, they had a car, or rather Cierra's brother had a car and Cierra had a set of keys she described as "basically mine." And the road across from the laundromat, it turned out, had real traffic on Saturdays: delivery vans, a church crowd at noon, and a stretch of angled curb between a fire hydrant and somebody's rusted Volvo that was, as Ms. Bui pointed out, exactly the length the examiners liked. Not quite as long as you'd want. That was the point.

On Saturday morning Gabrielle backed between the hydrant and the Volvo eleven times while Ms. Bui watched from her lawn chair with the air of a woman who could prognosticate failure from the angle of the first approach. She was right about nine of the eleven. The good ones felt strangely quiet, the wheel doing what her hands asked before her hands fully decided. The bad ones involved the curb, once, with a sound like a struck bell, and Tayla's voice from the back seat saying, "That's the earth's core."

The highway was the real opponent. Cierra drove them out to the on-ramp on Route 9 and pulled over at a gas station so they could switch seats, and Gabrielle sat for a moment with her hands at ten and two, looking at the ramp where the merge lane poured itself into three lanes of Saturday traffic. The trouble was timing. She kept flicking the signal on at the last second, as she started to move, the way you'd flick a light on entering a room. On her first attempt the car in the right lane leaned on its horn and Cierra said, evenly, "So that driver had, what, no warning. You signalled and moved at the same time."

"So I signalled," Gabrielle said. "I did the thing."

"You did half the thing." Cierra was looking in the mirror. "The signal's supposed to go on before, so the guy behind you gets a chance to slow down or make room. If it's on too late, or not at all, he's got no time to adjust. You have to tell people what you're about to do before you do it, not while you're doing it."

Gabrielle absorbed this with the particular resentment of someone hearing an obvious truth from a peer. Then she tried again. Signal first, mirror, blind spot, a full breath while the blinker ticked, and only then the wheel. A sedan drifted back to let her in, its driver raising two fingers off the wheel in a gesture she'd never received before, a small ceremony between strangers. She merged. It was, she thought, a little bathos after all that dread: the terrifying thing, done correctly, felt like almost nothing.

She drove forty minutes and exited and merged and exited again, and somewhere in the repetition the two ideas began braiding themselves together. Parallel parking was a private negotiation between her and the curb, an argument conducted at four miles an hour that nobody else could really help her win. Merging was the opposite, a public act, useless unless other people were given notice and time. She had been practising them as though they were the same skill, patience applied to metal, when really one asked her to be exact and the other asked her to be legible. She wasn't sure which was harder, and she said so, back in the laundromat parking lot with the engine ticking as it cooled.

Cierra considered it with the gravity of a philosopher who had never once framed it that way. "Or they're the same," she said, "because in both you're deciding how much space you're allowed to take." Tayla, from the back seat, said that was the kind of thing people said before they failed.

Ms. Bui was folding the lawn chair as they came in for the laundry nobody had actually done. She looked at Gabrielle for a long moment, the way she'd looked at her crossword. "The sixteenth," she said. "Eight in the morning. The curb will be empty because everyone will be at the diner." She paused with the chair half folded. "The Volvo's owner leaves for his daughter's at seven. You'll have the whole road to be bad on, if you get here at six-thirty."

"I'll be here at six," Gabrielle said, and went to check on the dryers.

activity: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
knowledge_domain: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
fact: The USDA recommends eating refrigerated cooked leftovers within three to four days, which limits how far ahead a week of meals can be cooked without freezing some.
story:
Amy's mother was leaving on Sunday night for a two-week course in Halifax, and before the taxi came she had to know that Amy could feed herself without living on toast. Amy had said, more than once, that she could plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches, and her mother had finally said, "Then show me," which was how Amy came to be standing in the kitchen on Saturday with a legal pad, three grocery store flyers, and a calculator that kept rounding wrong.

She worked it out with the seriousness of a lab report. Chicken and rice on Sunday, the same on Monday, a pot of lentil soup splitting Tuesday and Wednesday, pasta with the leftover chicken on Thursday, and the whole thing repeating until Friday, when she would allow herself frozen pizza as a reward for having survived. It was, she thought, a fairly cerebral victory: seven days reduced to three cooking sessions, a system, a grid. She copied the list onto a second sheet, checked the pantry for what she already owned, and found that she owned almost nothing except half a bag of rice and a tin of chickpeas with no label.

At the store she pushed the cart like someone conducting an experiment. She compared price per gram on chicken thighs, rejected a jar of sauce because her mother's rule about jars was unspoken but absolute, and stood in the spice aisle long enough that Marlee, who worked Saturdays at the checkout, waved her over. "You look like you're planning a heist," Marlee said. Amy showed her the grid on the legal pad, all seven days boxed and labelled, and Marlee turned it sideways as though the answer might be written somewhere in the margin. "Nice," she said. "Ambitious. What happens to day six?"

The question followed Amy home. Day six was Saturday, a week minus a day after she cooked, and it sat in the back of her mind all through Sunday afternoon while she browned the chicken and diced an alarming quantity of onion. She had the fridge open, sliding containers onto the shelf, when she noticed the note stuck to the door in her mother's handwriting, a note she had read a hundred times without reading: the note about leftovers. The USDA recommends eating refrigerated cooked leftovers within three to four days. Four days. Thursday at the outside, and her plan ran to Saturday. She stood there with a warm container in her hands, doing the arithmetic again as if the arithmetic might exoneration her plan somehow, as if the chicken thighs could be found not guilty of spoiling. They could not. Days five, six and seven were, by her own grid, a small food safety violation waiting to happen.

She called Sarah-Maude, who was the only person she knew whose family actually cooked like this. "So the USDA says three to four days for cooked leftovers in the fridge," Amy said. "My Friday stuff was cooked Sunday. That's day six." There was a pause on the line, then the sound of Sarah-Maude's younger brother yelling about something. "That's why my mom freezes half of everything," Sarah-Maude said. "The freezer stops the clock. Fridge, you get three to four days, so anything past that has to come out of the freezer instead." Amy looked at the freezer, at the ice-crusted tray of forgotten peas, at the two bags of bread heels her mother could never throw away. "I don't have room," she said. "You will if you eat the peas," Sarah-Maude said, and hung up because her brother had apparently escalated.

The reorganization took an hour. Amy ate the peas at eleven at night, standing at the counter, fork straight from the microwave bowl, because throwing them out felt like failing some test she had just invented. She stacked the bread heels on the counter to become breadcrumbs, which the internet said was possible, and cleared a shelf. Into it went Thursday's pasta in a labelled bag, and Friday's soup, and Saturday's portion, the labels written in her neatest hand with dates she now understood were not decorative. Her mother found her at midnight still in the kitchen, the legal pad revised, the old seven-day plan crossed through with a single line and rebuilt beneath it: fridge for the front half of the week, freezer for the back half, thawing times pencilled in the margin.

"Litotes," Amy said when her mother asked how it had gone. "You know. Saying 'not bad' when you mean good. That's what this was. Not bad." Her mother laughed, or something close to it, and looked at the labelled bags and the empty pea bowl and the grid with its two halves, and Amy understood that her mother was doing the same arithmetic she had done all afternoon, weighing the week ahead. In the morning her mother would be gone, and the system would have to survive contact with Amy's actual life, with rehearsals and tiredness and the Thursday she could already predict wanting takeout instead.

The taxi honked at seven. Amy stood on the front step holding a container of frozen soup her mother had insisted on taking for the flight, which defeated the entire purpose of the plan, and waved until the car turned the corner. Then she went back inside, opened the fridge, and moved Monday's chicken to the front of the shelf where she would see it first.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: The word valedictorian comes from the Latin vale dicere, meaning "to say farewell," which is why the valedictorian gives a farewell speech.
story:
The chairs on the football field had been set out in rows so straight they looked ruled, and Isabella sat in the third one from the aisle with her speech folded into quarters inside her gown pocket. The June heat pressed through the black polyester, and somewhere behind her a baby was crying in short, indignant bursts. In her pocket, the paper had gone soft at the folds already, from her hands.

She had not wanted to write a farewell. She had wanted to write about the physics wing, about the year the vending machine ate Kiara's dollar four times and the janitor pried it open with a screwdriver, about the smell of the biology lab on dissection day, which nobody would ever miss and everybody would somehow remember. But Mr. Nguyen had read her draft and said it was lovely and that it avoided saying goodbye entirely, and she had gone home and understood that avoidance was not the same as structure.

It was Isabela who gave her the way in. They had been in the library three nights ago, Isabela highlighting a page she wasn't reading, when Isabella said she didn't know how to end the speech without sounding like a greeting card. "Every ending I write is either confetti or a funeral." Isabela had spun her laptop around. She'd been looking up the word for a history paper and gotten sidetracked, the way she always did. "Valedictorian," she said. "It comes from the Latin vale dicere, to say farewell. That's the whole job. That's why you give the speech." Isabella had stared at the screen, at the small gray dictionary entry, feeling something loosen. The title she'd been proud of since September was not a crown at all. It was an assignment to say goodbye.

She had written a new ending that night at her kitchen table while her mother dried dishes behind her, and she had read it aloud once to the window, and then she had folded it up and stopped being sure. Because the Latin gave her permission to say farewell, but it didn't tell her what farewell meant when you were seventeen and the people in the folding chairs were scattering to eleven states and two countries and one gap year nobody's parents approved of. There was a version of goodbye that meant it's over, and a version that meant carry this with you, and she could not find the line between them, or whether a line existed.

Kiara leaned over from the next chair, her cap already crooked. "Nervous?"

"Corn," Isabella said.

"What?"

"If I say what I actually want to say, it'll be corn. If I don't, it'll be nothing." She pulled the folded paper halfway out of her pocket, then pushed it back. A memory surfaced, uninvited: junior year, the regional debate final, when she had cut her best argument in the last minute because the other team looked rattled and she wanted, for once, to be kind more than she wanted to win. She had lost by two points. She had never decided, in all the months since, whether it had been her finest moment or her most sentimental. Her coach had been furious; Mr. Nguyen, when she told him, had only nodded and said something about consequences you can't measure. She suspected both judgments were true at once, and that this was the kind of thing adults called maturity when they didn't want to admit there was no answer.

The principal was speaking now, his voice catching on the loudspeaker and arriving a half-second late, so his mouth moved before his words did. Then the orchestra, then the roll of names, each one followed by a small private eruption from some corner of the bleachers. Kiara crossed the stage and did a spin that made the vice principal smile against her will. Isabela walked with her chin high and her tassel already switched to the wrong side, out of impatience or rebellion, and Isabella watched her and thought about teleology, a word from Mr. Nguyen's class: the study of what things are for. The ceremony was for this, she supposed, the crossing, the name, the noise. But her speech was for the leaving, and the leaving hadn't happened yet, and she could not shake the feeling that she was delivering a verdict on something still in progress.

Then her name. The walk was longer than the field had ever seemed. The handshake, the leather folder, the stairs. And then the podium, the paper unfolding in her hands, the small crowd of nine hundred faces going quiet in patches, from the back forward, like a tide reversing. "Valedictorian," she began, "comes from the Latin vale dicere. To say farewell. Which means this speech is not an honor. It's homework." A laugh moved through the chairs, surprised and warm, and she felt her own nervousness break apart and rearrange itself into something she could stand on.

She read the middle part, the vending machine and the janitor and the biology lab, and the physics wing, and then she reached the ending she had written and stopped. Nine hundred faces. The baby had gone quiet. She looked down at the paper, then out at the folding chairs, at Kiara grinning with her cap crooked, at the exits where the parents stood, at the field she had crossed for four autumns. She skipped ahead three lines, folded the page in half, and said, "Some of you I will see again, and some of you I won't, and I've decided to be sanguine about which is which, since I clearly can't tell." Then, before anyone could applaud, before she could regret it, she stepped back from the microphone and held up the folded page, and the wind took one corner of it and lifted it, gently, like it was testing whether to take the whole thing.

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
knowledge_domain: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
fact: A 2002 study led by Richard Seager argued that winds and the ocean's seasonal heat storage, more than the Gulf Stream itself, explain most of Europe's mild winters.
story:
Vanessa had always thought of her grandfather's house as a place where the sea came indoors: rope coiled on hooks, a tide clock with a cracked face, and a wooden cabinet where he kept his charts, rolled and pale as onion skin. She came that Saturday with her textbook, her notes, and a problem she could not solve alone. Her report for Ms. Rosen's class was due Tuesday, and its central claim, copied neatly at the top of her first page, was that the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe. It sounded right. Everyone said it. But Jayda had sent her a photograph of a paragraph from a study the night before, and the paragraph had knocked the sentence loose from its footing.

"Read this again," Vanessa said aloud to the empty kitchen, unrolling the photograph on her phone. Jayda had been effusive about the find, texting six messages in a row, certain she had uncovered a scandal. The study, led by a scientist named Richard Seager, had come out in 2002, and it argued that winds and the ocean's seasonal heat storage, more than the Gulf Stream itself, explained most of Europe's mild winters. Vanessa read it four times. It did not say the Gulf Stream did nothing. That was the part that kept snagging her, the difference between nothing and less than people think.

Her grandfather came in smelling of coffee and salt, saw the charts already spread on his table, and raised an eyebrow at her.

"You're the one who wanted to learn current maps," he said. "Sit, then. Don't desensitize yourself to them before you've learned to feel them. Most people look at a chart once and think they've seen the ocean."

She did not entirely know what he meant, but she sat. He unrolled a chart of the North Atlantic and weighted its corners with mugs. The paper was the substrate of a whole craft, she realized, lines and arrows and depth numbers laid down on it the way a town is laid on land. He showed her how the arrows clustered along the eastern edge of North America, warm water pouring northward, then bending east across the ocean toward Europe. "Follow it with your finger," he said. "Don't skip. The finger remembers what the eye skims."

Her finger traced the current. It was a river inside the sea, warmer than the water around it, and it moved with a slowness that startled her. "How fast?" she asked.

"Walk speed, some of it," he said. "Faster in places. You'd drown in it and never be pulled anywhere dramatic. It's not a conveyor belt like the pictures make it look."

That was not helping her problem. She told him about the report, about the sentence she had written, about Jayda's paragraph. He listened with his hands folded, which was how he listened when he was genuinely interested.

"So which is it?" Vanessa said. "Does the stream warm Europe or not? My whole report says it does. One paragraph says mostly it doesn't, or mostly it's not the main thing, and I can't tell which one I'm supposed to believe."

"Who says you're supposed to believe either one clean?" he said. "I fished that water forty years. The current is real. Your finger just followed it. But weather comes from above more than below, most days. Wind decides where the warmth sits." He tapped the chart north of Scotland. "Both things can be true, girl. The question is how much of each."

Vanessa pulled her notebook over and drew two columns. In one she wrote what the old explanation gave her: a warm river, drawn on every chart in the cabinet, the story everyone told. In the other she wrote the 2002 study: winds and the ocean's seasonal heat storage carrying more of the weight, the Gulf Stream less. She sat looking at the two lists, waiting for one to collapse, and neither did. Was that a failure of the lists or a failure of the world to be simple? She noticed, slowly, that she was not disappointed. She was curious. If the familiar story was too big, what else had she been carrying around at the wrong size?

Anika arrived at noon with her bike helmet still on and half a granola bar in her hand, because Anika never fully finished arriving anywhere. She read the two columns upside down from across the table. "So your report is wrong," she said.

"It's not wrong," Vanessa said. "It's incomplete. There's a difference and I think the difference is the whole assignment." She looked at her grandfather, who was pretending to be busy with the kettle. "I want to say the Gulf Stream carries warm water toward Europe. That's true, it's on every chart here. Then I want to say a 2002 study led by Richard Seager argued that winds and the ocean's seasonal heat storage, more than the Gulf Stream itself, explain most of Europe's mild winters. Then I want to say I don't know yet how the two fit together, and that nobody in my class knows either, including me."

"You'll get marked down," Anika said, chewing.
